First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Until August 1996 the occupiers bombed the towns and villages of Ichkeria, killed Chechen civilians and held them without charges in filtration camps.

In the autumn of 1991, during the collapse of the USSR, Chechens overthrew the Soviet authorities installed in the Chechen-Ingush Republic, elected Dzhokhar Dudayev president and declared the independence of the Chechen Republic. Russia did not recognize it and was preparing a coup[1].

In the autumn of 1994, Russia armed the Provisional Council, a puppet opposition, to overthrow Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria. The Russian army handed the council 10 armored personnel carriers, 40 tanks and 6 combat helicopters with their crews. Officers of the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) recruited Russian tank crews for the council (see: "Staging a Coup")[1]. On 1 October the Moscow newspaper Kommersant wrote that the Russian Ministry of Defense "imperturbably rejects all accusations, stating that it has nothing to do with the events taking place in Chechnya"[2]. On 26 November the defenders of Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, routed the Russian tank crews who were storming the city under the banner of the puppet opposition, and took dozens of Russian servicemen prisoner[1]. On 1 December Russian pilots destroyed all of Ichkeria's aircraft on the airfields[3]. On 9 December Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2166, ordered the government to use all means of the Russian state, including the army, against the Armed Forces of Ichkeria[4].

The Russian columns moved into Ichkeria a day before the talks that Russia had scheduled for 12 December 1994 (see: "Negotiations as Cover for an Attack")[1]. Sources differ: some put the strength of these columns at 14,972 men, others at almost 24,000[5][6]. On the day of the invasion, Yeltsin promised in an address to the citizens of Russia: "I oblige all officials responsible for carrying out the measures to restore constitutional order in the Chechen Republic [this is what Russia called its war against independent Ichkeria] not to use violence against the civilian population and to take it under protection"[1]. Seven days after the address, from 18 December, Russian aircraft bombed the residential districts of Grozny. Deinekin, the commander of the Russian military aviation, said in an interview with the newspaper Moskovsky Komsomolets on 21 March 1995 that the pilots dropped unguided bombs on the city through the clouds when "the ground could not be seen at all"[1]. On 31 December the Russian army stormed Grozny. The defenders of the city routed the occupiers' columns. On 19 January 1995 Russian soldiers captured the ruins of the presidential palace and stormed the remaining districts of the city for another month and a half, until 6 March[1]. By early February 1995 Russia had brought the number of its troops in Ichkeria up to 70,000 men[7]. The Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations interviewed 265 refugee families from Grozny. By the mission's estimate, from December 1994 to March 1995 the occupiers killed 25,000-29,000 civilians in the city (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1].

At the end of March 1995 the Russian army captured Argun, Gudermes and Shali, towns to the east and southeast of Grozny[1]. On 7 April soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and police officers stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 8 April the occupiers searched the houses. Sadulla Yusupov, an elderly Chechen from Samashki, told Oleg Orlov of the Russian human rights organization Memorial on 13 April: "They were screaming in inhuman voices, swearing, cursing, shouting: 'Come out, you bitches!' and they went up to every house and fired"[8]. The Observer Mission published a list by name of 103 people whom the occupiers killed in the village in two days (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[8]. In June Russian troops captured Vedeno, Shatoy and Nozhai-Yurt, district centers in the mountains in the south (see: "Military Intervention")[1][9].

On 14 June 1995 fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria took about 1,500 hostages in Budyonnovsk, a Russian-controlled town to the northwest of the republic, and demanded an end to the war. Five days later Russia began talks with Ichkeria in Grozny[1]. On 3 July, while the talks were under way, Yeltsin, by Decree No. 663, allowed units of the Russian army "to be stationed on a permanent basis" in the republic[10]. On 30 July the delegations of Russia and Ichkeria signed an agreement on the cessation of hostilities. Russia undertook to withdraw its troops as the army of Ichkeria handed over its weapons[11][12]. Chechen fighters began to hand over weapons, but the Russian units did not leave the republic[1]. On 6 October unknown persons seriously wounded Romanov, the commander of the occupation troops, in Grozny. The next day the leadership of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria called the attempt a provocation aimed at wrecking the peace agreement[13]. On 9 October Yeltsin blamed the attempt on "supporters of [Dzhokhar] Dudayev" (the elected president of the Chechen Republic), and Russia resumed its offensive[1].

From February to May 1996 the Russian army stormed the settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria and the villages of Sernovodsk, Samashki and Bamut in the west (see: "Military Intervention")[1]. In the spring Russian commanders signed "Protocols on Peace and Accord" with villages[1]. A village undertook not to let fighters of the army of Ichkeria in, and Russia promised not to conduct combat operations in it[14]. Contrary to the agreements, Russian pilots bombed villages that had signed the protocols (see: "False Guarantees of Safety")[1]. On 21 April 1996 the Russian military struck a clearing near Gekhi-Chu, a village to the southwest of Grozny, with missiles and killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")[15][1]. On 27 May Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, signed a ceasefire agreement in Moscow. On 10 June in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, Russia undertook to withdraw its troops from the republic by the end of August 1996[1][16]. On 9 July, six days after Yeltsin won the Russian presidential election, the occupiers launched a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")[1].

Russian servicemen and police officers took detained Chechens without charges to filtration camps and to pits at military units (see: "Filtration Camp System"). According to a memorandum by Zlydenko, the deputy head of the prison service of the Russian MVD, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995, 1,325 people passed through the camps in Grozny and in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia. The ministry released most of them as innocent and handed one hundred over to investigators (see: "Manufacturing Criminals"). The Russian MVD gave another 141 people to be exchanged for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Hostage-Taking")[1]. In September 1995 the UN Special Rapporteur on torture wrote to the Russian government that many inmates of the camps were systematically beaten to extract a confession of support for Dzhokhar Dudayev (see: "Torture and Abuse")[17]. According to statements by relatives collected by the Chechen society "Victims of War", 1,285 people were listed as missing in June 1996 (see: "Abduction of People")[1]. In January 1998 the UN Working Group on Enforced Disappearances reported that Russia had not established the fate of a single missing person about whom it had been asked[18].

Russian officials and military officers called the authorities of Ichkeria "bandits"[19][20], its army "bandit formations"[1] and "terrorists"[21][22], and Chechen civilians "bandits"[23] and "militants" (see: "Dehumanization")[24]. Generals of the occupation troops passed off the civilians they had killed as fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions")[1].

Russia kept no count of the civilians it killed in Ichkeria[1]. On 3 September 1996 General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, named the total number of those who died in the war at a press conference in Moscow: 80,000 people, "give or take 10,000"[25][26]. In its annual report for 1996 the international human rights organization Human Rights Watch estimated the number of civilians killed in Ichkeria since December 1994 at 18,500 to 80,000[27]. In a 1995 resolution the European Parliament condemned Russia's use of the army against Ichkeria[28]. In a 1995 declaration the Parliamentary Assembly of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe called Russia's war in Ichkeria a gross violation of international law[29]. On 25 January 1996 the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions wrote in a report to the UN Commission on Human Rights that the Russian military had killed thousands of citizens of Ichkeria, including when they deliberately and indiscriminately shelled residential districts with heavy weapons and bombed them[30]. Memorial concluded that Russian troops deliberately attacked civilians throughout the war and killed the most of them by bombing and shelling[1].

A Human Rights Watch report of January 1997 says that Russia systematically violated human rights and just as systematically failed to bring the perpetrators to justice[31]. On 12 March 1997 the deputies in Moscow, by Resolution No. 1199-II, declared an amnesty for crimes connected with the war in Ichkeria. Under this amnesty Russian prosecutors closed unfinished cases on the crimes of the occupiers[32][1]. On 29 September 1997 the Directorate of Military Courts of Russia replied to a request from Memorial that over the whole war the courts had convicted 18 Russian soldiers and officers, seven of them for murder (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[1].

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[9]. On 31 August 1996 General Lebed and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed the peace agreements in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan. In them Russia acknowledged "the inadmissibility of the use of armed force or the threat of its use in resolving disputed issues". The agreements state that the decision on the independence of Ichkeria was postponed for five years, until 31 December 2001 (see: "Sham Treaties")[33]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic. On 27 January 1997 the citizens of Ichkeria elected the president and parliament of the republic. Aslan Maskhadov became president[1]. Three years after the Khasavyurt agreements Russia attacked Ichkeria for the second time since 1994. On 21 September 1999 Russian pilots began bombing Grozny, and on 29 September the Russian army invaded the republic[1].

T0005 Aggressor Claiming Victim Status
September 1994
C1193.T0005 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0008 Government

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia presented its attacks as a forced response and shifted the blame for the war onto Ichkeria.

Russian President Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the government, Defense Minister Grachev and the commanders of the occupation troops declared the offensives of the Russian army a response to attacks and provocations by the army of Ichkeria, and blamed the leadership of Ichkeria for the breakdown of negotiations[1]. The commanders said this to journalists of Russian news agencies, radio and television[1][34].

On the night of 29 November 1994, Russian President Yeltsin declared that the fighting in Ichkeria could not be stopped, and threatened to use all the forces of the state if the army of Ichkeria and the puppet opposition did not lay down their arms within 48 hours[35][36]. Russia itself had armed the puppet opposition and led it into battle, and on 29 November the Security Council of Russia decided to start the war[1].

On 18 February 1995, during the "ceasefire", Russian artillerymen shelled the positions of the army of Ichkeria near Shali, Argun and Gudermes, towns to the east of Grozny, and the defenders did not return fire (see: "Sham Ceasefire")[1]. On 19 February, the Russian government declared that the army of Ichkeria had attacked Russian units on the southern outskirts of Grozny and wrecked the negotiations[1][37].

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 7 and 8 April, the occupiers killed 103 peaceful Chechens in the village (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[8]. On the evening of 7 April, Russian television channels, citing the military, reported that fighters of the army of Ichkeria had shot the village elders. That day, Russian soldiers had fired on the cars in which the elders were travelling, and all eight people survived (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions")[8]. On 1 May 1995, Sergei Kovalyov, a deputy of the Russian parliament, said at a hearing in the US Congress that this report had served as a pretext for a punitive action against the village[38]. In July 1995, six of the ten deputies of the Russian parliament's commission that investigated the causes of the war wrote in their conclusion that the command of the occupation troops had decided to storm Samashki "after yet another killing of three servicemen (border guards)"[8][39][40]. The border guards had been killed in January 1995, three months before the storming, in the neighboring stanitsa of Assinovskaya[8].

After unknown persons made an assassination attempt in Grozny on 6 October 1995 on Romanov, the commander of the occupation troops, Russian President Yeltsin on 9 October and Defense Minister Grachev on 10 October blamed the attempt on supporters of Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria. Russia suspended negotiations with Ichkeria and ordered the troops to resume the offensive[1][41]. On 14 December, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Gudermes, the second-largest town of the republic, and the occupiers stormed it until 20 December and killed at least 267 townspeople (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[1]. On 26 December, Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, stated that whoever opens fire first is to blame for the deaths, and that the fighters of the army of Ichkeria attack first[34].

In January 1996, the Russian government wrote to the UN Secretary-General that Russia had from the very beginning wanted to settle the matter by negotiations, and that supporters of Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, were wrecking the peace process with provocations[42]. In late January, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, in a letter to deputies of the Russian parliament, blamed the leadership of Ichkeria for the breakdown of negotiations and promised to launch propaganda before new strikes on the republic. The head of the government warned that casualties were inevitable, including among peaceful Chechens[1].

On 7 May 1996, the crews of five Russian helicopters fired rockets at Urus-Martan, a town south-west of Grozny where there had been no fighting for a year and a half, and killed five Chechens at the market (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1][43]. Fatima Ashgerieva, who was travelling by bus to Urus-Martan that day, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "We did not hear a single shot from the direction of Urus-Martan, only shots from the helicopters"[24]. On 10 May, Russian pilots again killed one Chechen in Urus-Martan and seriously wounded eight, among them four children. On 12 May, the crews of Russian helicopters killed 20-year-old Khasmagomed Arsemikov and wounded eight women[1][24].

On 12 May 1996, Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, justified the strike on Urus-Martan on the Vesti program of the RTR television channel: "There was at the same time an attempt to provoke actions by the federal [Russian] troops… And at the same time fire at the helicopters. Which, of course, provoked retaliatory actions by the federal troops"[1]. On 13 May, officials of the Russian-controlled Urus-Martan district said on the Vremya program of the ORT television channel that there were no armed units in the town and that no one had fired at the Russian helicopters[44]. On 13, 14 and 17 May, police of the occupation administration and the Russian military searched houses in Urus-Martan but did not find a single fighter of the army of Ichkeria[1].

On 9 July 1996, a month after Russia and Ichkeria agreed on a ceasefire in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, the occupiers began a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")[16]. On 17 July, while Russian pilots were bombing the surroundings of Shatoy and Vedeno, villages in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, stated that Ichkeria had been the first to resort to provocation, contrary to the agreements signed in Moscow and Nazran[1].

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[9]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan (see: "Sham Treaties")[33]. Three years later, on 21 September 1999, Russian pilots began bombing Grozny, and on 29 September the Russian army invaded the republic again[1]. Russia officially called the new war a "counter-terrorist operation"[1].

T0006 Dehumanization
September 1994
C1193.T0006 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0008 Government

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Throughout the war, Russia called the army and the authorities of Ichkeria "bandits", "bandit formations" and "terrorists", and Chechens "militants".

On 2 November 1993, Russian president Yeltsin, by decree No. 1833, approved a military doctrine under which the army could be used against "illegal armed formations"[45][46]. With these words Russian officials designated the Armed Forces of Ichkeria[1].

On 27 December 1994, Russian president Yeltsin, in a televised address to the citizens of Russia, called some of the defenders of Ichkeria professional "terrorists" and mercenaries from other states. The president set Russian soldiers and police officers the task of disarming the "bandit formations". Yeltsin warned Russians that their relatives could fall victim to the "rampant banditry" in Ichkeria[47]. Commanders of the occupation forces called the people in Grozny and in the villages that the Russian army was pounding "bandit formations" and "militants"[1].

A soldier of the Russian border troops who fought in Ichkeria told the newspaper Rossiyskiye Vesti about retraining in Stavropol, a city in the south of Russia. There the soldiers were told to set booby traps without thinking about who would be blown up by them: a child would grow up to be a "mujahid", and a woman would give birth to a new "militant"[1].

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) began the assault on Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria[8]. On 8 April, a Russian soldier was driving women and children out of a cellar on Vygonnaya Street. Mariet T., a Chechen woman from that street, told observers of Memorial that the occupier shouted at them: "These aren't women, they're bitches, whores, they kill ours too, and we're supposed to spare theirs?!" Then the Russian military herded some of the women into a room and others into a cellar and shot at them (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). Ruslan N. from Samashki recalled how MVD soldiers detained him that day: "They took my passport and right there, in front of me, tore it up… 'You'll go down as a militant. You've got a militant's mug'". At a military unit north of the village, the servicemen beat him unconscious. Ruslan N. survived[48].

Russian officials and military men, from the prime minister to the soldier conducting a search, called the authorities of Ichkeria "bandits"[19][20], its army "bandit formations"[1] and "terrorists"[21][22], and Chechen civilians "bandits"[23] and "militants"[24]. On 4 January 1996, Tikhomirov, commander of the occupation forces, in an interview with the Russian agency Interfax, spoke of Aslan Maskhadov, chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, as a "bandit"[1].

On 11 and 12 July 1996, unknown persons blew up two trolleybuses in Moscow[1]. According to Amnesty International, at the site of the second explosion Moscow mayor Luzhkov told a Russian police general that all Chechens should be expelled from the city. The general replied that if he were allowed to, he would introduce terror on the streets. The Russian television channel NTV showed this conversation on the day of the explosion[49][1]. At a press conference at the mayor's office, Luzhkov told journalists that a "Chechen trace" could be seen in the explosions[50][51][1]. Alexander Litvinenko, a former FSB officer, and the historian Yuri Felshtinsky write that those who blew up the trolleybuses "were not caught and… it was not determined whether they were Chechens or not"[52]. Human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch wrote in their report for 1996 that Luzhkov's televised statements "set the tone" for raids on markets and dormitories. In the two days after the explosions, the Moscow police, which verified documents "overwhelmingly against dark-skinned people", detained 5,770 people for violating residence registration rules[27]. In a 1999 report, Amnesty International wrote that for several years Luzhkov's statements served the police as an implied instruction to persecute and intimidate Chechens solely because they were Chechens[53].

At a hearing in the US Congress, the Russian journalist Yevgenia Albats said that those whom Russia called "bandits" were ordinary citizens who had stood up for their land, their houses and their families[38]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that until June 1995, and again from late January 1996, Russia waged the war without calling it a war or the enemy an enemy[1].

T0007.001 Lies about Its Own Actions
September 1994
C1193.T0007.001 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0008 Government

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Throughout the war, Russian President Yeltsin, Russian ministers and generals denied the crimes of the occupation troops, attributed them to the army of Ichkeria, and passed off peaceful Chechens killed by the Russian military as its fighters.

On 1 December 1994, ten days before the open invasion, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, by Directive No. 1886-r created the Temporary Information Center (see: "Censorship")[54]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that the center almost immediately began to spread disinformation and to obstruct the work of Russian and foreign journalists in Ichkeria[1].

To inquiries from UN rapporteurs and deputies of the Russian parliament, the Russian government, the command of the occupation troops and the military prosecutor's office replied that the soldiers had been attacked by the army of Ichkeria and that no reports of crimes had been received[30][1].

Russian ministers, generals and press services denied that the army had fought in Ichkeria in the autumn of 1994[55][56][57][58][1], and that pilots had bombed Grozny in December 1994[1][23][3]. On 4 February 1995, Russian Justice Minister Kovalyov said that he and his colleagues had visited Ichkeria and had not found a single case of looting by Russian soldiers[1].

The operational headquarters of the Russian government and the Russian military attributed to the army of Ichkeria the destruction of residential districts of Grozny in December 1994[59][1] and the killings of peaceful people in the towns of Shali in January 1995[60][1] and Gudermes in April 1995[1].

Russian President Yeltsin promised to stop the bombing or declared the fighting over on 27 December 1994[1], 19 January 1995[19][61], 10 May 1995[62] and 5 April 1996[24], and Chernomyrdin, chairman of the government, on 17 July 1996[1]. After each statement, Russian troops went on bombing and storming the villages and towns of Ichkeria[1][24].

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 7 and 8 April, the occupiers killed 103 peaceful Chechens in the village (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[8]. On the evening of 7 April, the first channel of Russian television and the NTV television channel, citing the Interfax news agency and the Russian military, reported that fighters of the army of Ichkeria had shot the village elders. That day, Russian soldiers had fired on the cars in which the elders and the mullah were returning from negotiations. All eight people in the cars survived. On 11 April, five elders of Samashki handed human rights defenders of Memorial a statement: "The statement of the military leadership of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs is a fabrication from beginning to end"[48]. On 29 May, the Russian parliament's commission investigating the causes of the war in Ichkeria found the reports of the shooting of the elders to be a lie[8].

On 8 April 1995, the ITAR-TASS news agency reported that Russian troops had killed more than 130 fighters of the army of Ichkeria in battle in Samashki. On 11 April, a representative of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs told an NTV correspondent of 120 fighters killed by the Russian military and said that the peaceful Chechens had left before the storming. That day, Soskovets, deputy chairman of the Russian government, answered an NTV correspondent's question about the killings of women and men in the village: "No, there is nothing of the kind"[8]. Russian investigators in the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, offered Makhmudemin Iziev from Samashki to sign testimony that the Chechen fighters had fired first. On 18 April, the Russian military released him without charges[1][8]. Govorukhin, chairman of the Russian parliament's commission investigating the causes of the war, told the deputies after his trip to Samashki on 14 April that he had counted there "about fifty destroyed or damaged houses"[8]. On 1 May 1995, the human rights defender Sergei Kovalyov said at a hearing in the US Congress that his group of human rights defenders had compiled a list of 374 destroyed houses in the village[38]. In July, some members of the Russian parliament's commission wrote a conclusion in the name of the whole commission: "men must be excluded from the list [of Chechens killed in the village]. People who held an assault rifle or a grenade launcher in their hands cannot be considered peaceful residents". The report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights defenders says that in this way the deputies recorded all the men of Samashki as fighters of the army of Ichkeria. The Mission named all 103 Chechens killed by the occupiers - 90 men and 13 women. Four of them had held weapons in their hands[8]. On 15 August 1995, the Russian government replied to the UN Special Rapporteur on torture that the houses in Samashki had been destroyed by fighters of the army of Ichkeria, and that the military prosecutor's office had received no reports of executions of Chechens without trial[17].

Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, denied the bombing of the village of Roshni-Chu in October 1995[63]. Russian generals denied the shelling of the settlement of Novogroznensky in February 1996[1]. Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, stated in March 1996 that the military prosecutor's office had received no reports of looting[1], and in April 1996 denied that his subordinates had killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria[1].

Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, gave a figure of 267 casualties among the townspeople of Gudermes, which Russian troops stormed in December 1995. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that this figure is greatly understated[1]. Russian Defense Minister Grachev recorded as fighters of the army of Ichkeria the peaceful Chechens whom his troops killed in the settlement of Novogroznensky in February 1996[1]. A representative of the Russian military attributed to Chechen fighters dressed in Russian uniforms the looting that Russian soldiers carried out in the village of Sernovodsk in March 1996 (see: "Pillage")[1].

On 28 March 1996, a Russian pilot dropped a bomb on Katyr-Yurt, a village south-west of Grozny, and killed nine people of the Khazhgiriyev family (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The next day, Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, according to the Interfax news agency, admitted that the crew had bombed without orders and apologized to the family[1][64]. On 31 March, Russian President Yeltsin, in an address to the citizens of Russia, promised to halt the offensive. On the night of 3 April and on 4 April, Russian pilots bombed Shalazhi, a village south-west of Grozny, and killed three Chechens[1][24]. Deinekin, the commander of the Russian Air Force, and Tikhomirov called the bombing a provocation[1]. On 10 April, Deinekin said at a press conference shown by the Vesti program of the RTR television channel: "neither Katyr-Yurt, nor Shalazhi twice, nor any other populated areas were bombed or planned to be bombed by the federal Air Force [the Russian air force] and army aviation". The general added that the bombs in the villages were being set off by fighters of the army of Ichkeria[1]. Kureysh Khazhgiriyev, a Chechen from Katyr-Yurt whose relatives were killed by the Russian pilot, said on 22 April to the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow: "I cannot bear to hear General Deinekin blasphemously declare that they did not bomb. I have no words! Shame on the general"[24]. Russian prosecutors suspended the cases on the bombings of Katyr-Yurt and Shalazhi (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators"). In November 1997, the military prosecutor's office of Russia admitted in a letter to Memorial that Katyr-Yurt had been bombed by an aircraft of the Russian troops, and of Shalazhi wrote that Russian aviation had struck the army of Ichkeria there[1].

Generals of the occupation troops denied the shelling of the town of Urus-Martan in May 1996[43][1]. A representative of Russian aviation denied the bombing of the Nozhay-Yurt district in the south-east of Ichkeria on 3 June 1996, the third day of the ceasefire agreed by Russia and Ichkeria[1][65]. In July 1996, Russian soldiers held detained Chechens in pits in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny. That month, Solovyov, the military prosecutor of the Russian troops in the North Caucasus, replied to Yuly Rybakov, a deputy of the Russian parliament, that he had found no unofficial filtration camps. By 5 August, the occupiers had released the detainees[1].

Commander Tikhomirov recorded as fighters the peaceful Chechens whom Russian pilots killed in the town of Shali in April 1996[1]. The headquarters of the occupation troops attributed to the army of Ichkeria the shelling of the town of Urus-Martan in May 1996, in which the crews of Russian helicopters killed townspeople[1][24]. The Russian military repeatedly stated that the army of Ichkeria was defending itself in mosques and cultural monuments. Isa Adayev, director of the National Museum of the Chechen Republic, told the public tribunal of the Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996 that this was untrue[24]. General Shamanov, who commanded the storming of the village of Makhkety, recorded as fighters of the army of Ichkeria the peaceful Chechens whom Russian troops killed there in July 1996[1][9].

In August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had encircled the occupiers in Grozny, the command of the occupation troops and Russian Defense Minister Rodionov declared that they controlled the center of the city[1][66].

Human rights defenders of Memorial write that many reports by Russian newspapers, radio and television about atrocities of the army of Ichkeria, citing official Russian sources, turned out on checking to be lies[1].

On 21 November 1997, almost a year after the last Russian troops had left Ichkeria, Smirnov, deputy chief military prosecutor of Russia, wrote to Memorial that Roshni-Chu had been bombed by eight attack aircraft whose affiliation the prosecutor's office had not established. The prosecutor denied that in August 1996 soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Ministry of Internal Affairs had taken Chechen men hostage at the "15th Gorodok", their base in Grozny. The brigade released the men when their relatives met its demands (see: "Hostage-Taking")[1].

T0007.002 Occupation as Salvation
September 1994
C1193.T0007.002 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0008 Government

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Throughout the war, Moscow declared the invasion and occupation a blessing for the Chechens.

On 30 November 1994, Russian president Yeltsin signed secret decree No. 2137 "On Measures to Restore Constitutional Legality and Law and Order on the Territory of the Chechen Republic" (that is what the colonizer called the preparation of the attack on Ichkeria)[1]. On 9 December, by decree No. 2166 the president instructed the Russian government to use all means "to ensure… the rights and freedoms of citizens"[4].

On 27 January 1995, Yeltsin signed decree No. 79 "On Ensuring the Conditions for the Re-creation of Constitutional Organs of Power in the Chechen Republic" (see: "Installation of a New System of Governance")[1][67]. On 12 July 1996, the fourth day of the occupation troops' offensive, the president, by decree No. 1028, named as constitutional organs the government that Moscow had installed in Grozny (see: "Puppet Government")[1][67][50].

On 11 December 1994, the day of the open invasion, Yeltsin addressed the citizens of Russia: "Our goal is to find a political solution to the problems of one of the subjects of the Russian Federation — the Chechen Republic, and to protect its citizens from armed extremism." The president of Russia promised: "I oblige all officials responsible for carrying out the measures to restore constitutional order in the Chechen Republic [that is what Russia called its war against independent Ichkeria] not to use violence against the civilian population and to take it under protection"[1]. A week later, from 18 December, Russian pilots bombed Grozny, and from 19 December until the storming on 31 December they bombed it every day. Human rights defenders of the Russian organization Memorial write: "The bombs and missiles fell mainly on neighborhoods where residential buildings stood and where there were knowingly no military objects" (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. By the estimate of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations, from December 1994 to March 1995 the occupiers killed 25-29 thousand civilian townspeople in Grozny (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[1].

On 11 January 1996, the Russian government replied to the UN Secretary-General's inquiry about human rights in Ichkeria that an extremely complex situation had forced Moscow to use armed force. The reply says that on 29 August 1995 Yeltsin appointed Lobov, secretary of the Russian Security Council, as his representative in Ichkeria to guarantee human rights and prepare free elections (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")[42].

On 23 April 1996, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, stated at a meeting of the government commission on settling the war: "The UN Charter also contains the concept of 'peace enforcement', and in this case it can be applied"[1]. Two days later, on 25 April, Russian pilots bombed Shali, a town southeast of Grozny that the occupation troops had surrounded six days earlier (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The occupiers killed Chechen civilians and, according to the report of the head of the Shali district to the Interfax agency, wounded 29 people[1]. Eleven days later, on 6 May, Russian troops seized Shali without a fight and found no defenders there (see: "Collective Punishment")[1].

On 17 July 1996, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, stated at a meeting of the government commission on settling the war that in six months Russia had liquidated the "anti-constitutional regime" (that is what Russia called the government of Ichkeria) that had threatened its territorial integrity[1].

T0008 Deprivation of Agency
September 1994
C1193.T0008 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0008 Government

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia did not recognize Ichkeria as an independent state, nor its elected president and government as a party to the war and to negotiations.

On 9 December 1994, two days before the open invasion, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, by Resolution No. 1360 ordered the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Defense to disarm the "illegal armed formations" (as Russia called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria)[68]. On 17 December, Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2200, created a Russian administration for Ichkeria. On 20 December, the Russian government, by Resolution No. 1411, obliged all enterprises, organizations and institutions of the republic to carry out the decisions of this administration (see: "Installation of a New System of Governance")[1].

Throughout the war, the president, ministers and generals of Russia refused to negotiate with the leadership of Ichkeria or demanded that it first surrender its weapons and disband its army[1].

On 1 February 1995, Ilyushenko, acting Prosecutor General of Russia, charged Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of Ichkeria, with high treason, calls for terrorism, violation of national and racial equality and violation of the law on referendums[69]. The Prosecutor General's Office of Russia issued a warrant for the arrest of the Chechen president and put him on the all-Russian wanted list[1].

On 30 July 1995, Russia signed an agreement with Ichkeria on the cessation of hostilities. The Russian delegation added to its first line that Ichkeria was not recognized by the legislation of Russia[11][12].

On 12 December 1994, the day after the open invasion, the Russian delegation at the negotiations in Vladikavkaz, the capital of North Ossetia, demanded that the representatives of Ichkeria recognize the republic as part of Russia[1].

On 17 December 1994, Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, informed Yeltsin by telegram that he had ordered a ceasefire against the Russian troops and proposed to begin negotiations without preconditions, which he would lead himself[70]. On 18 December, Yeltsin by telegram ordered the president of Ichkeria to appear that same day in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, at the headquarters of the occupation troops and to sign a document on the surrender of weapons and a ceasefire[70][1]. The press service of the Russian president told the Russian news agency ITAR-TASS that further telegrams from the Chechen president would not be answered[71]. On 23 December, Dzhokhar Dudayev conveyed through Sergei Kovalyov, the Russian human rights commissioner, to Russian Foreign Minister Kozyrev that he was ready to cease fire immediately and to negotiate on everything, including the disarmament of the army of Ichkeria, but received no answer from Moscow[1]. On 27 December, Yeltsin, in a televised address to the citizens of Russia, declared: "the regime in Grozny [as the Russian president called the government of Ichkeria] is illegal", and of negotiations he said: "The subject of negotiations is a ceasefire and the surrender of weapons"[47][1]. On 31 December, the Russian army began the storming of Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")[1].

On 18 January 1995, Russian President Yeltsin said on Russian television that he would not talk to Dzhokhar Dudayev[1]. From February to June 1995, Russian Defense Minister Grachev and Kulikov, the commander of the occupation troops, replied to the proposals of a ceasefire from Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, that they would talk only about the surrender of weapons and the disbanding of the army of Ichkeria[72][1][73]. On 19 May 1995, Yeltsin rejected the law by which, on 12 April, Russian deputies had instructed the Russian government to begin direct negotiations with the leadership of Ichkeria immediately and without preconditions[1][74]. On 5 July 1995, two weeks after negotiations with Ichkeria began in Grozny, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, and the Russian negotiators declared that they would not discuss its status[1].

On 10 January 1996, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, said: "Chechnya is Russia"[75]. On 11 January, the Russian government, in a letter to the UN Secretary-General, named the government of Ichkeria as the cause of the war, declaring it illegal and Ichkeria itself part of Russia[42]. On 7 April, Mikhailov, Russian minister for nationalities, said that the parties to the negotiations should be the commanders of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria. On 17 April, Russian Justice Minister Kovalyov declared that direct negotiations with Dzhokhar Dudayev, "a subject of criminal proceedings", were impossible, and invited him to come to a Russian court. On 21 April, the Russian military killed the president of Ichkeria (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition"). On 25 April, Justice Minister Kovalyov announced that negotiations with the commanders of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria would be conducted by the puppet government in Grozny[1].

On 27 May 1996, Russian President Yeltsin received in the Kremlin, for negotiations on a ceasefire, a delegation of Ichkeria headed by Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, acting president of Ichkeria. The Russian organizers of the meeting assigned the representatives of Ichkeria seats at the side of the table, while Yeltsin sat at its head. Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev demanded to sit opposite the Russian president, as at negotiations between two states, and to Yeltsin's "Sit down" he replied across the negotiating table: "I will not sit down to that tone". The Russian president moved to the middle of the table[76]. The Russian delegation did not write the names of the parties into the ceasefire agreement, and Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev signed it with their surnames and no titles. Mikhailov, Russian minister for nationalities, explained this to journalists at a press conference at the Russian news agency Interfax: "If we had written 'Ichkeria', that would practically mean recognizing the existence of a republic that does not exist..."[76]. On 28 May, the Russian organizers of the meeting did not let the delegation of Ichkeria meet with Moscow journalists, and in the evening the delegation flew to Russian-controlled Ingushetia[1].

On 25 July 1996, General Pulikovsky, acting commander of the occupation troops, told journalists that with the commanders of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria he would discuss only the place and time of the surrender of weapons[77]. On 28 July, Pulikovsky replied on air on the Russian television channel RTR to Aslan Maskhadov's proposal to discuss ending the war that he did not know where to look for the leadership of Ichkeria[78][1].

Human rights defenders of Memorial write that the president and government of Russia called the war their internal affair[1].

On 31 August 1996, General Lebed, secretary of the Security Council of Russia, and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan, the agreements on the withdrawal of the occupation troops (see: "Sham Treaties"). Russia and Ichkeria postponed the decision on the independence of Ichkeria for five years, until 31 December 2001[33][1]. The word "Ichkeria" does not appear in the agreements: the republic is called the Chechen Republic[33]. In September 1999, the Russian army invaded Ichkeria for the second time since 1994[1].

T0019 Military Intervention
September 1994
C1193.T0019 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers captured the towns and villages of Ichkeria.

On 26 November 1994 the defenders of Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, routed the Russian tank crews who were storming the city under the banner of the puppet opposition (see: "Staging a Coup")[79]. By 29 November the Russian army had gathered about 140 combat aircraft for the attack on Ichkeria. On 29 November Russian pilots in six Su-27 aircraft and four helicopters attacked the presidential palace in Grozny[80]. On 1 December the crews of Russian Su-25 attack aircraft destroyed all of Ichkeria's aircraft on its airfields[3]. On 9 December Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2166, ordered the government to use all means of the Russian state, including the army, against the Armed Forces of Ichkeria[4].

A day before the talks between Russia and Ichkeria scheduled for 12 December, the Russian army and the Internal Troops of the MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) began an offensive in three columns from the neighboring Russian-controlled republics (see: "Negotiations as Cover for an Attack")[1]. Sources differ: some put the strength of these columns at 14,972 men, others at almost 24,000[5][6]. The Russian Ministry of Defense estimated the Armed Forces of Ichkeria at 11,000-12,000 fighters, the Russian MVD at up to 15,000, and both ministries counted another 30,000-40,000 Chechen volunteers[7]. The northern column advanced from Mozdok, and the western column from Vladikavkaz through Ingushetia. The eastern column set out from Kizlyar, a town in Dagestan[1][68]. On 11 December unarmed Chechens of the Khasavyurt district of Dagestan surrounded the armored personnel carriers of the eastern column and did not let the occupation troops through[81][1]. On 12 December near the village of Novy Sharoy in the west of Ichkeria, thousands of Chechens stood on the road in front of the western column and held it up for a week at the border with Ingushetia[1][82]. On that day the army of Ichkeria stopped the northern column near the settlement of Dolinsky, about ten kilometers northwest of Grozny[1].

Before a storming, Russian troops surrounded towns and villages and shelled them with artillery, while Russian aircraft bombed them (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. The occupiers demanded that the Chechens in the surrounded villages expel the defenders and hand over their weapons (see: "Collective Punishment")[1]. In the captured towns Russian troops set up commandant's offices and garrisons. In Grozny Russia installed the Russian-controlled "Government of National Revival" (see: "Puppet Government")[1][9].

From 18 December 1994 Russian aircraft bombed the residential districts of Grozny. On 19 December units of the Russian airborne division from Pskov under the command of General Babichev reached the western outskirts of the city[1]. On 31 December the Russian army stormed Grozny from four sides. The defenders of the city routed the occupiers' columns and took more than a hundred Russian servicemen prisoner. The human rights defenders of Memorial write about the troops of General Pulikovsky, who were advancing from the northwest: "The 131st (Maikop) Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade and the 81st (Samara) Motorized Rifle Regiment were almost completely routed"[1].

On 7-9 January 1995 the occupiers stormed Grozny again, from the north and west. Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the vice president of Ichkeria, who together with Aslan Maskhadov led the defense of the presidential palace, wrote in his memoirs about the evening of 18 January: "We were deciding one question: to stay and die, which was tantamount to the destruction of the Main Staff, or to leave the Presidential Palace and set up a new headquarters on the other side of the Sunzha [the river in the center of Grozny]"[56]. On the night of 19 January Russian pilots dropped concrete-piercing bombs on the palace, and the defenders were forced to leave. On 19 January Russian soldiers captured the ruins of the palace. The occupiers stormed the remaining districts of Grozny for another month and a half. By early February 1995 Russia had brought the number of its troops in Ichkeria up to 70,000 men[7]. The defenders fought longest in Chernorechye in the south of the city, and on 6 March 1995 the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD captured this district[1].

On 23 March 1995 the occupiers captured Argun, a town to the east of Grozny[1]. On 24 March Russian troops broke into Achkhoy-Martan, a district center in the west of Ichkeria, but fighters of the army of Ichkeria liberated the village with a counterattack[9]. On 28 and 29 March the Russian army surrounded Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, and Shali, a town to the southeast of Grozny. Russian commanders demanded that the townspeople persuade the defenders to leave, and on 30-31 March, when the fighters of the army of Ichkeria were forced to leave both towns, the occupiers captured them without a fight[1]. On 12 May the Russian army began an offensive into the mountains in the south of Ichkeria. On 3 June the occupiers captured Vedeno, a district center to the southeast of Grozny, and on 12 June Shatoy to the south of the capital and Nozhai-Yurt in the southeast[9][1]. On 18 June 1995 Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, agreed on a cessation of fighting with Shamil Basayev, the commander of the fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria who had taken hostages in Budyonnovsk, a Russian-controlled town to the northwest of the republic. That evening the occupation troops halted their offensive (see: "Sham Treaties")[1]. At the end of July, Grozny, Argun, Gudermes, Shali and the mountain district centers were under occupation by the Russian army, while in most villages there were no Russian troops[1][9]. On 14 December 1995 the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Gudermes to disrupt the "vote" for the head of the puppet government. On 19-20 December, after six days of shelling and bombing of residential districts, the occupiers captured the town again[1][34].

On 17-20 February 1996 the Russian army shelled and captured by storm Novogroznensky, a settlement to the east of Gudermes[1]. On 3 March Russian troops broke into Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, on the day their commanders had set for signing a peace with the leaders of the village, and the defenders drove the attackers out. By 9 March, after six days of shelling, the defenders of Sernovodsk were forced to leave, and the occupiers captured the village[1]. On 6 March the Armed Forces of Ichkeria under the command of Ruslan Gelayev attacked the occupiers in Grozny and liberated most of the city. The army of Ichkeria did not try to hold the city and left it on 8 March[1][9]. On the night of 14 March Russian troops surrounded Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and on 15 March began a storming with tanks, artillery, helicopters and aircraft. On 19 March the fighters of the army of Ichkeria under the command of Khizir Khachukayev ran out of ammunition and were forced to leave[1]. On 4 April, after six days of bombing, Russian soldiers broke into Goyskoye, a village to the southwest of Grozny, but the defenders under the command of Akhmed Zakayev repelled the storming. On 7 May the occupiers under the command of General Shamanov captured Goyskoye[1]. On 24 May, after three months of stormings, shelling and bombing, the Russian army captured Bamut, a village in the west of Ichkeria at the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia, while the defenders under the command of Ruslan Khaikhoroyev broke out of the encirclement[1].

On 9 July 1996, six days after the Russian presidential election, the occupiers violated the ceasefire agreement signed with Ichkeria on 27 May and launched a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")[1]. On that day Russian units under the command of General Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, surrounded and shelled Gekhi, a village to the southwest of Grozny, where a unit of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria was stationed. By 12 July the occupiers had killed the unit's commander Doku Makhayev and destroyed more than a third of the village[83]. On 15 July the occupiers captured Makhkety, a mountain village of the Vedeno district in the southeast of Ichkeria, which they had surrounded five days earlier[1][9].

The Russian human rights defenders of Memorial write that the Russian army with aircraft, heavy artillery and tanks fought against Ichkeria, although the president and government of Russia passed the war off as a police disarmament[1]. On 19 January 1995 the European Parliament in a resolution condemned Russia's use of the army against Ichkeria[28]. The Parliamentary Assembly of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in a declaration of 8 July 1995 condemned Russia's war in Ichkeria as a gross violation of international law[29].

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers. In three days of fighting the army of Ichkeria retook the center and about 80 percent of the city[9]. The defenders forced Russia to the negotiating table. On 22 August 1996 in the village of Novye Atagi in the south of the republic, Russia and Ichkeria signed an agreement on the withdrawal of Russian troops from Grozny and joint control over certain districts of the city[1][84]. On 31 August 1996 General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed a joint statement in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan. In it Russia acknowledged that resolving disputed issues by force or the threat of force was inadmissible (see: "Sham Treaties")[33].

By 31 August 1996 the occupation troops had left Grozny for their main bases in Khankala on the eastern outskirts of the city and at the Severny airport to the north of it. Russian police officers and soldiers of the Internal Troops of the MVD remained in the city. Russia withdrew its troops from Vedeno, Shatoy, Nozhai-Yurt and Kurchaloy, villages in the south and east of Ichkeria. Russian units still stood in Shali, near Bamut and in the Naur and Shelkovskaya districts in the north of Ichkeria[9]. In these two districts beyond the Terek river there was no fighting during the whole war. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1].

T0020 Staging a Coup
September 1994
C1193.T0020 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0017 Secret Police and Security Services

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian special services and the army gave the puppet opposition money, weapons, instructors, tank crewmen and pilots in order to overthrow Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of the Chechen Republic.

In the summer of 1994, Russia's Ministry for Nationalities Affairs and the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) helped the puppet opposition recruit armed fighters in Znamenskoye, a village in the northwest of Ichkeria, and in Urus-Martan, a town southwest of Grozny[1]. Russia allocated more than 150 billion rubles to the Provisional Council, the leadership of the puppet opposition, which it had confirmed at a congress on 3 June. In an analytical memorandum, the FSK named the head of the Provisional Council the most suitable candidate for support[1].

On 3 September 1994, the Russian government, in an address to the Chechen people, proposed that Dzhokhar Dudayev resign[1].

On 5 September 1994, the General Staff of the Russian army ordered that 10 armored personnel carriers and 6 combat helicopters with crews be handed over to the Provisional Council[1]. From these helicopters, Russian pilots fired rockets at residential houses in Ichkeria (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). In November, the Russian army handed tanks over to the council[1][85].

In September and October 1994, Russian officers trained more than a hundred fighters of the Provisional Council to drive T-62 tanks and fire army mortars at the "Prudboy" training ground near Volgograd, a city in the south of Russia[86][1].

In October 1994, Savostyanov, the head of the Moscow directorate of the FSK, ordered that Russian soldiers and officers who knew how to maintain armored vehicles and fight in them be found for the Provisional Council. The military counterintelligence of the FSK selected the candidates[87]. From 3 to 9 November, FSK officers travelled around military units near Moscow and signed contracts with tank crewmen[1][87].

In November 1994, Kolesnikov, the Chief of the General Staff of the Russian army, authorized sending the recruits to the Caucasus. Kotenkov, Russia's deputy minister for nationalities affairs, directed the dispatch, and by 16 November the recruits had been brought to Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia near the border of the Chechen Republic[1]. Russia denied that it was sending its servicemen to fight for the Provisional Council (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions").

In the autumn of 1994, FSK officers fought on the side of the puppet opposition[1].

From September 1994 until the assault on Grozny on 26 November, fighters of the Provisional Council and Russian crews attacked Ichkeria. On 2 September, fighters of the council and a column of twelve tanks with Russian crews attacked Grozny. The Armed Forces of Ichkeria stopped them at the settlement of Dolinsky, northwest of Grozny, knocked out a tank and took eight men prisoner, among them, according to initial reports, Russian servicemen[88][55][82][1][89][90]. On 30 September, Russian pilots in four helicopters of the Provisional Council fired rockets at the "Severny" airport in Grozny and destroyed five civilian aircraft and two aircraft of the army of Ichkeria, and fighters of the puppet opposition blocked the entrances to the city[1][2][91]. Dzhokhar Dudayev rejected the Provisional Council's ultimatum to surrender within six hours, and the council's fighters dispersed without attacking Grozny[2][92]. On 15 October, fighters of the Provisional Council stormed Grozny from the south and from the north, and the Armed Forces of Ichkeria repelled the assault. The defenders took several dozen attackers prisoner, among them, according to various reports, 12 to 15 Russian officers[92], and on 16 October the council's fighters retreated to their bases in Znamenskoye and in Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny[1].

On 17 November 1994, nine days before the assault on Grozny, a group of Russian officers headed by Kolesnikov, the Chief of the General Staff, flew from Moscow to Mozdok[1]. Valery Yakov, special correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia, wrote about the preparation of the assault in November 1996: "There, in Mozdok, at the 'Arsenal' base, the contract soldiers [recruited Russian servicemen]… trained the Chechen crews [of the Provisional Council]… In all, the contract soldiers received 40 brand-new tanks, 16 of which had 'Russian' crews"[93][87]. On 26 November, fighters of the Provisional Council and Russian tank crewmen under the command of Zhukov, the deputy commander of a Russian army corps from Volgograd, stormed Grozny[1][87]. Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the vice president of the Chechen Republic, wrote in his memoirs that in the morning he saw the start of the assault from the window of his office in the presidential palace: "on the northeastern outskirts of the city, from the direction of Tolstoy-Yurt [a village north of Grozny where the fighters of the Provisional Council were stationed], tank and artillery fire began to thunder"[56]. The tanks reached the center of Grozny, where fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria shot them up with grenade launchers[1]. The defenders routed the attackers and, according to the government of the Chechen Republic, took 68 Russian servicemen prisoner[94]. Among the prisoners were soldiers and officers of the Russian Kantemirovskaya Tank Division from near Moscow[57].

Human rights defenders of Memorial write that without Russia's military help the puppet opposition could not have overthrown Dzhokhar Dudayev[1].

After the defeat of 26 November, the Provisional Council withdrew its fighters to its bases[9][1]. Fifteen days later, on 11 December 1994, the Russian army openly invaded the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")[1].

T0021 Neutralization of the Opposition
September 1994
C1193.T0021 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0017 Secret Police and Security Services

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia killed the leaders of Ichkeria, put them on wanted lists and arrested the republic's representatives in Moscow.

Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 1226 of 14 June 1994, allowed anyone suspected of ties to criminal groups to be held without charge for up to 30 days[95]. Under this decree, the FSB and the Russian police detained representatives of Ichkeria in Moscow[96][68].

On 1 February 1995, the Prosecutor General's Office of Russia put Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of Ichkeria, on the wanted list in order to arrest and try him (see: "Manufacturing Criminals")[1].

On 17 June 1995, officers of the FSB and the Moscow police arrested Khamad Kurbanov, the representative of the president of Ichkeria in Russia, and two days later Ramzan Muzaev, secretary of the Chechen news agency Chechen-Press[96]. The FSB and police officers held both without charge, released the agency's secretary by 26 July, and the president's representative a month after his arrest[95][97][24]. On 8 October 1995, during the "ceasefire", Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, and killed 28 people, among them Magomed Khachuev, head of security of the delegation of Ichkeria at the talks. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that the target of the strike was Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, who at times lived in the village and was unharmed[1].

On 21 April 1996, Dzhokhar Dudayev, with his wife Alla Dudayeva, his associates and his guards, drove out of Gekhi-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, to a clearing in the mountains. The president put a satellite phone on the hood of the car and called Konstantin Borovoy, a deputy of the Russian parliament and a mediator in the peace talks. Russian servicemen struck the clearing with missiles[98]. The occupiers killed the president of Ichkeria, Prosecutor General Magomet Zhaniev and Khamad Kurbanov, the republic's former representative in Moscow. Alla Dudayeva was standing twenty meters from the car. In her memoirs, the president's wife wrote: "Suddenly, from the left, came the sharp whistle of an incoming missile. The explosion behind my back and the yellow flame that flared up made me jump down into the ravine... but suddenly the whistle came again"[15].

On 21 and 22 April 1996, Russian troops struck six or seven headquarters of the leadership of Ichkeria in the mountains with missiles and bombs[1]. Alexander Litvinenko, a former FSB officer, wrote in 2002 that the killing of the president had been prepared by an FSB group under the command of Khokholkov, created "to eliminate Dudayev", in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny. According to him, aircraft of Russian military intelligence guided the missile to a beacon in the president's substituted phone[52].

On 7 May 1996, Russian police officers secretly detained Vagap Tutakov, Ichkeria's representative in Moscow, as he was leaving Kaluga, a city southwest of Moscow[1]. The police officers claimed that they had found weapons in his car[99], and on 8 June they released Ichkeria's representative from custody[1]. On 10 July 1996, Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, ordered a search for and the detention of Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria[1][9]. That same day, Russian pilots and artillerymen struck Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev's headquarters in Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria[1]. On 15 July, the occupiers captured Makhkety but did not find the acting president there[9]. That day, the crews of seven Russian helicopters destroyed his mother's house in Starye Atagi, a village south of Grozny, with missiles; the mother and the neighbors survived (see: "Collective Punishment")[9][83].

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[9]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[33]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1].

T0023 Filtration Camp System
September 1994
C1193.T0023 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0017 Secret Police and Security Services

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers unlawfully detained Chechens and held them without charges in filtration camps and in pits at military units.

On 12 December 1994, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs created filtration camps by directive No. 247. The ministry set them up in prison railcars in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, in the prisons of Stavropol and Pyatigorsk, cities in the south of Russia, and in the building of a motor depot in Grozny[1][100].

Russian servicemen together with police officers detained Chechens at checkpoints and during "zachistki" ("sweeps", as Russians called house searches and detentions of Chechens). In its detention orders, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs most often referred to the decree of the president of Russia of 2 November 1993 No. 1815 "On Measures to Prevent Vagrancy and Begging"[101]. The decree concerned vagrants, while most of the detained Chechens had their documents on them[1].

Before sending them to the camps, the occupiers held Chechens for several days in pits and prison vans at checkpoints and at their bases, in places with no official status[1]. There were such pits in the 503rd and 506th regiments of the Russian army near Shali, a town southeast of Grozny[24][1]. From February 1995, the occupiers brought Chechens to Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, and from there sent them to Mozdok[1].

In the camps, Russian guards beat and tortured detained Chechens during interrogations, including with electric current (see: "Torture and Abuse"). The guards did not treat the wounded[100]. The occupiers did not let detained Chechens tell their relatives where they were. For their families, the people went missing (see: "Abduction of People")[1].

The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs released most of the detained Chechens from the camps as innocent. From each of them the ministry took a signature saying they had no complaints[1].

According to a certificate by Zlydenko, deputy head of Russia's prison service, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995, 1,325 people passed through the camps in Mozdok and Grozny. The Ministry of Internal Affairs handed a hundred of them over to investigators (see: "Manufacturing Criminals"). The ministry gave another 141 people up for exchange for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Hostage-Taking")[1].

During the storming of Grozny in early January 1995, the Russian troops of General Rokhlin detained men in the bomb shelters near the cannery, where they were hiding from the shelling, and took them to Mozdok[100]. On 3 January, the guards carried more than 60 of them in the back of a single truck and killed at least eight on the way (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")[1]. On 10 January, the Chechen Umar Kasayev died in the Pyatigorsk prison: the Ministry of Internal Affairs did not give him the medical care he needed[100].

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Officers of the FSK (the predecessor of today's FSB) flew in to the Russian checkpoint near the village with lists of Chechens "subject to filtration"[48][8]. On 8 April, soldiers of the Internal Troops and of police special units from Orenburg and Moscow searched the houses of Samashki. By 10 April, the occupiers had unlawfully detained and taken out of the village more than 200 Chechen men aged 15 to 70, and the escort shot three of them dead on the way (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")[48][1]. Azman Ansarova from Samashki told the "Memorial" observers that when one of the detained men showed a soldier his passport, "he took the document and tore it to shreds. 'I don't need your documents,' he says. 'You are Chechens — we are going to kill you'… Then they took our sons and drove them away"[8]. The occupiers sent some of the men by helicopter to Mozdok and held others in pits and prison vans near Assinovskaya. On 5 August 1995, Khasan Rasuyev from Samashki told "Memorial" how the guards loaded the detainees into the back of a truck: "And in stacks — into the back. In four layers, I think, one on top of another"[1][8]. Near Assinovskaya, the Russian military released most of the men without certificates of detention, and from Mozdok, by 18 April, the Ministry of Internal Affairs had released 65 Chechens from Samashki as innocent and given 12 up for exchange[1][8].

In April 1995, Russian servicemen took the brother of the Chechen woman Khaza Arsanukayeva from his home in Grozny at night, citing his residence registration in Kalmykia, a Russian-controlled republic by the Caspian Sea. The soldiers beat him at the headquarters of the occupation troops and took him to the filtration camp on the northeastern outskirts of the city, and a week later the guards released him: he could not walk[23].

On 15 March 1996, at the checkpoint near Samashki, the occupiers picked out 91 Chechens from among those leaving the village before the assault and took them to the prisons of Pyatigorsk and Stavropol. Five weeks later, the Ministry of Internal Affairs released them without charges[1]. In March 1996, soldiers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs detained three Chechens at the checkpoint between Goity and Starye Atagi, villages south of Grozny, and on 7 April Russian servicemen took the Chechen Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village near Grozny. The Russians held all four in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, and exchanged them for their own captured soldiers (see: "Hostage-Taking")[31].

In its 1995 comments, the UN Human Rights Committee expressed concern at reports of torture, ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in filtration camps[102]. In early 1997, the human rights defenders of "Memorial" wrote that Russian agencies "are not making substantial efforts to search for Chechens who were detained and went missing"[103]. "Memorial" published the accounts of detainees and lists of Chechens whom the Ministry of Internal Affairs held in the prisons of Pyatigorsk and Stavropol from January to February 1995[100].

On 10 June 1996, in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, Russia undertook before Ichkeria to close the filtration camps and the other places where it unlawfully held Chechens[104]. In June, the Ministry of Internal Affairs closed the last camps[1]. Russian courts convicted no one for creating the camps and for the unlawful detentions (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")[1].

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table[9]. On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")[33]. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic[1].

T0025 Information Isolation
September 1994
C1193.T0025 →
C1193 First Russian-Chechen War (1994–1996)
G0011 Russian Federation
S0010 Regular Army

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers bombed Chechen television, jammed journalists' satellite links and kept them away from the sites of their strikes.

Commanders of the occupation forces ordered that journalists not be let into the sites of assaults and bombings. The Russian military and police at checkpoints did not let journalists, including those with accreditation from the Russian government, into the villages and towns that Russian troops were striking (see: "Censorship")[1][24]. Human rights defenders of the American Committee to Protect Journalists write that Russian troops in Ichkeria jammed journalists' satellite transmissions, exposed their film and destroyed their equipment[105].

On 29 November 1994, Russia announced that at 2 p.m. it would cut off all communications with Ichkeria[35]. From 21 to 24 December, Russian pilots struck the television center in Grozny. Deinekin, commander of Russian military aviation, named the aim of these strikes: "to stop the rabid anti-Russian propaganda"[1].

On 3 January 1995, Russian pilots bombed Shali, a town southeast of Grozny. Human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch write that the pilots were apparently trying to hit a radio communication tower, but killed several townspeople at the market and in the hospital (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[72]. On 7 and 8 April, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 Chechen civilians there (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")[8]. On 11 April, the occupiers at the post near the village did not let journalists in and admitted them only on 13 April[48][8]. On 8 October, Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The occupiers blocked all the roads to the village, and men of the police special forces from the Russian city of Irkutsk at the post did not let journalists in, citing an order[1][106]. From 11 December, before the "elections" of the head of the puppet government on 14-17 December, Russian soldiers at checkpoints did not let journalists without special passes into Grozny (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")[1]. From 14 to 20 December, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, the second-largest city of the republic, the occupiers shelled and bombed the city, and until 25 December did not let the press in (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[34].

In January 1996, the command of the occupation forces closed Grozny and the east of Ichkeria to the press[34]. From February until the first days of March, the occupiers shelled with artillery the encircled settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria and the villages of Alleroy, Tsentoroy, Bachi-Yurt and Suvorov-Yurt (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The Russian military did not let journalists in there[1]. From 3 to 9 March, Russian troops shelled Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, with artillery and fired on it from helicopters (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[1]. From 6 to 9 March, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were attacking the occupiers in Grozny, Russian officials did not let journalists into the city[105]. On 10 March, the Russian military commandant of Sernovodsk forbade letting journalists, human rights defenders and any foreigners into the village (see: "Expulsion of Foreign Missions")[1].

On 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Russian 58th Army began the assault on Samashki (see: "Military Intervention")[1]. Sources differ on the number of Chechen civilians the occupiers killed in the village during the assault: 35 according to the villagers' list[1] or about 600 according to a doctor who treated people there (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")[9][24]. On 17 and 18 March, the occupiers did not let independent journalists from Moscow through to the village. Maria Eismont, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Segodnya, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April that on 26 and 27 March the Russian military stopped her on the roads to Samashki, and that she got into the village five days later. In Sernovodsk, Russian soldiers who had taken part in the assault turned the journalists back with the words: "There's no need to go there, there's nothing for you to do there, all the more so since there is nothing at all left to look at." Alexander Trushin, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Obshchaya Gazeta, told the Glasnost tribunal on 21 April that in early April the chief of the Russian checkpoint near the village phoned a general and did not let the journalists through: "I asked the captain: 'Did you report why we are going, for what purpose?' He answered: 'Yes, the general knows, and nevertheless the order is not to let you through'"[24]. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that reports of this assault did not reach television and radio[1].

On 21 April 1996, the occupiers killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, during his conversation on a satellite phone with a mediator in the peace talks; according to the version that human rights defenders of Memorial consider likely, the Russian military located the signal of this phone (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")[98][1]. On 8 August 1996, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, Russian soldiers did not let four journalists of foreign media into the city through either of its two entrances[105].
